method: Independent fact-check. WebSearch (standard mode) was used for every item flagged by the writer and for every title/author/year, 'first', 'founded' and 'named after' claim. WebFetch was not usable, so search-result summaries are the only web source (no primary pages were read). Lint: node scripts/library-profile-check.mjs --staging prints OK for all three files after the edits.

softened.was: Norman Corwin's On a Note of Triumph (1945) showed the medium's ambition.
softened.now: Norman Corwin's On a Note of Triumph (1945) is often cited as showing the medium's ambition.
softened.why: Date and CBS broadcast on 8 May 1945 confirmed; the 'ambition' line is a characterisation and is now attributed to common opinion.

softened.was: became the best-known radio play ever
softened.now: became one of the best-known radio plays ever
softened.why: Superlative cannot be verified. October 1938 Mercury Theatre broadcast, Welles/Koch credit and the 'panic smaller than newspapers reported' argument were confirmed (the panic claim is already worded as an argument).

softened.where: tropes conv 7 (Under Milk Wood as chorus)
softened.was: Under Milk Wood is the standard example
softened.now: Under Milk Wood is a well-known example
softened.why: 'The standard example' is an opinion, not a checkable fact.

softened.was: Louis MacNeice's verse play The Dark Tower (1946)
softened.now: Louis MacNeice's radio play The Dark Tower (1946)
softened.why: Year 1946, BBC Home Service and Britten's music confirmed (broadcast date given as 21 or 26 January 1946 by different pages), but I could not be sure the play is wholly in verse, so the genre label was reduced to 'radio play'.

softened.now: the Neues Hörspiel from the late 1960s
softened.why: Kagel's Ein Aufnahmezustand (first part 1969) and Kriwet's Apollo Amerika (1969) are the usual early examples; the movement is described as late-1960s onward. Kagel and Kriwet as Neues Hörspiel figures confirmed.

softened.was: Pace by ear: people speak at roughly 120 to 160 words a minute
softened.now: Pace by ear: as a rule of thumb people speak at roughly 120 to 160 words a minute
softened.why: Not a sourced figure; now labelled a rule of thumb.

softened.was: Where scripted drama is heard on radio today it is mostly on public broadcasters; elsewhere it has moved to on-demand audio,
softened.now: Scripted drama on radio today is largely the work of public-service broadcasters in several countries; elsewhere it has moved to on-demand audio,
softened.why: General statement from memory, not sourced; made country-specific and less absolute.

softened.was: spot effects are those made live in the studio as the scene is performed, as against effects played from recordings.
softened.now: spot effects are individual sounds tied to one action, such as a door or a telephone, traditionally made live in the studio as the scene was performed.
softened.why: Search found 'spot effects' used for discrete action-tied sounds; the 'made live' sense is traditional British studio usage but usage varies, so both are stated and the live sense is marked 'traditionally'.

confirmedNotes: A Comedy of Danger: Richard Hughes, BBC, 15 January 1924, set in a Welsh coal mine when the lights go out; the 'first play written for radio' label is disputed (record stays contested).
Zauberei auf dem Sender: Hans Flesch, Frankfurt, 24 October 1924; Rolf Gunold's Spuk (27 January 1925, Breslau) named as a rival candidate in German sources.

Third Programme opened 29 September 1946; Under Milk Wood first broadcast on it 25 January 1954 (Richard Burton as First Voice); All That Fall 13 January 1957 (Maddy walks to the station to meet blind Dan); A Slight Ache 29 July 1959 on the Third Programme, stage 1961.

The Archers: pilot week from 29 May 1950 on the Midlands Home Service, national from 1 January 1951, created by Godfrey Baseley; widely described as the world's longest-running drama ('one of' is safe).
Suspense and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar both ended on CBS on 30 September 1962; CBS Radio Mystery Theater 6 January 1974 to 31 December 1982.

Hitchhiker's Guide: BBC Radio 4, first episode 8 March 1978; novel October 1979. Sorry, Wrong Number: Lucille Fletcher, Suspense, 25 May 1943 (one source gives 18 May; year 1943 not in doubt), bedridden woman, telephone.
Radio Ballads: eight programmes 1958 to 1964 by Ewan MacColl, Peggy Seeger and Charles Parker; The Ballad of John Axon 2 July 1958.

Günter Eich's Träume: NWDR, broadcast 19 April 1951. Soap opera name from soap-maker sponsors: confirmed. Play for voices as the Under Milk Wood subtitle: confirmed. Sting, atmos, segue definitions consistent with standard usage.
remainingDoubts: Only search-result summaries were available (WebFetch could not reach hosts); no primary pages (BBC Genome, CBS logs) were read.
The Dark Tower: exact broadcast day (21 or 26 January 1946) differs between pages; the text gives only the year, and whether it is wholly verse was not settled.
Whether the Radio Ballads are best described as 'documentary-drama' (canon conv 6) is a characterisation.
Spot effects usage differs between British studio practice and general sound-design usage; the glossary line now allows both.
Speech-rate figure, slot lengths (15/30/45/60 minutes), and the 'public broadcasters' statement remain general practice, not sourced statistics.

corrected.was: Podcasting began in 2004, when audio downloads by subscription and the name podcast appeared,
corrected.now: Podcasting took shape in the early 2000s and got its name in 2004,
corrected.why: Search sources place the technical groundwork (RSS enclosures, audio-by-feed experiments) in 2000 to 2003, the name in early 2004, and mainstream adoption in 2005 with iTunes 4.9 (28 June 2005); no source dates 'the beginning' to 2004 alone. No coiner is named.

corrected.where: canon conv 1 (label for Alice Isn't Dead)
corrected.was: Mock broadcast: Welcome to Night Vale (2012) ..., and Alice Isn't Dead (2016), Fink's horror serial ... from the Night Vale Presents label.
corrected.now: Mock broadcast and the Night Vale Presents label: Welcome to Night Vale (2012) ..., and Alice Isn't Dead (2016), Fink's horror serial narrated by a long-haul truck driver.
corrected.why: Alice Isn't Dead (first episode 8 March 2016, Night Vale Presents, narrated by a long-haul truck driver, Jasika Nicole) is not a mock broadcast; it was filed under that heading only because of the label, so the heading now says so.

softened.was: Its documentary manner of a reporter-host, interviews and tape shaped fictions such as Limetown (2015)
softened.now: Its documentary manner of a reporter-host, interviews and tape was echoed by fictions such as Limetown (2015)
softened.why: A direct causal claim of influence cannot be sourced; 'echoed' is descriptive.

softened.was: that moves from comedy toward a darker plot.
softened.now: that mixes workplace comedy with a darker plot.
softened.why: Characterisation; now matches the subgenres wording. Run confirmed: first episode August 2014, final episode 25 December 2017 (4 seasons).

softened.was: a growing number of shows publish transcripts,
Content notes are commonly given: producers often state heavy subjects
softened.now: Content notes are often given: producers may state heavy subjects
softened.why: General-practice claim; softened (the text already says practice varies by show and platform).

confirmedNotes: Big Finish founded 1996, first audio plays late 1998 (Bernice Summerfield), first Doctor Who play (The Sirens of Time) 1999.
iTunes podcast support: iTunes 4.9, 28 June 2005. Escape Pod: first episode 12 May 2005 (one page lists 16 May), weekly science-fiction short stories.
Welcome to Night Vale: first episode 15 June 2012, Joseph Fink and Jeffrey Cranor; Night Vale Presents founded 2015 (successor to Commonplace Books).

Limetown: July/August 2015 (pages give 21, 26, 29 July or 2 August; the text says only 2015), Zack Akers and Skip Bronkie; Facebook Watch series premiered 16 October 2019 and was cancelled January 2020, so the writer's '2019, not 2018' is right.
Homecoming: Gimlet, November 2016, Eli Horowitz and Micah Bloomberg; Amazon series 2 November 2018; Spotify's purchase of Gimlet reported 6 February 2019.
The Magnus Archives: 24 March 2016 to 25 March 2021 (one fan page gives 23 March), five seasons, 200 episodes, Jonathan Sims.
Archive 81: Dan Powell and Marc Sollinger, 2016 start supported by Netflix's own Tudum article and other pages (one page says 2019, treated as an error); Netflix series premiered 14 January 2022.

Audible's The Sandman: released 15 July 2020, adapted and directed by Dirk Maggs. Podiobook term attributed to Evo Terra of Podiobooks.com (the text does not name a coiner). Foley named for Jack Foley.
remainingDoubts: Only search-result summaries were available (no primary pages read).
Archive 81: one search result gave 2019 for the podcast start; the 2016 date is the better-supported one but no primary source settled it.
Limetown's exact first-episode date varies by source; the text gives only the year.
'Homecoming told largely through conversations and calls' and 'Alice Isn't Dead ... horror serial' are characterisations from memory plus a quick check.
Diegetic and binaural glossary lines are standard but were not checked against a published glossary.
Episode-length, release-rhythm, content-note and transcript statements in the readers facet remain general-practice claims, not sourced statistics.

corrected.was: new producers made shows for download from the start, such as 99% Invisible (2010), a design show that grew from a San Francisco radio project.
corrected.now: shows such as 99% Invisible (2010), a design show that grew from a short San Francisco radio feature, found their audience by download.
corrected.why: The original sentence contradicted itself: 99% Invisible began on 3 September 2010 as a short KALW and AIA San Francisco radio feature, so 'made for download from the start' was wrong.

corrected.was: This American Life (1995), created by Ira Glass, the template
corrected.now: This American Life (1995), hosted by Ira Glass, the template
corrected.why: Reference pages credit Ira Glass and Torey Malatia as creators; 'hosted by' is true without the credit question. The works entry (author Ira Glass) matches the library's own entry and is unchanged.

softened.was: reached an audience far beyond earlier public radio podcasts
softened.why: Comparative claim unsourced. Premiere 3 October 2014, Sarah Koenig, This American Life team, one case across a season: confirmed.

softened.was: which its makers described as a novel in form.
softened.now: which was widely likened to a novel in form.
softened.why: Release of all seven chapters on 28 March 2017 confirmed; reviewers and a producer compared it to a novel, but the exact wording attributed to the makers could not be confirmed.

softened.was: which treated a podcast as a literary narrative.
softened.now: and often likened to a novel.
softened.why: Characterisation made consistent with the history line.

confirmedNotes: Murrow's 1940 London reports (live, during the Blitz); Studs Terkel's WFMT programme 1952 to 1997 (earlier name The Wax Museum per WFMT; Britannica gives a 1998 end, text uses 1952 to 1997 as WFMT and Wikipedia do).
NPR: incorporated 1970, broadcasting from 1971 (All Things Considered 3 May 1971; one page dates the first broadcast to April 1971).

This American Life: first aired 17 November 1995 on WBEZ as Your Radio Playhouse, renamed within months. The Moth: founded 1997 by George Dawes Green in New York. Radiolab: Jad Abumrad, 2002, WNYC; Krulwich co-host from about 2004 to 2005.

99% Invisible: first episode 3 September 2010, KALW and AIA San Francisco. In the Dark: APM Reports, Madeleine Baran, first episodes 7 September 2016, season one on Jacob Wetterling. Revisionist History: Malcolm Gladwell, June 2016, Panoply, later Pushkin Industries.
Radio Ballads and The Ballad of John Axon author string confirmed against credits (script MacColl and Parker, music direction Seeger, production Parker).
remainingDoubts: Only search-result summaries were available (no primary pages read).
Studs Terkel end year: 1997 (WFMT, Wikipedia) versus January 1998 (Britannica).
Radiolab: Krulwich's joining date differs between pages (2002 meeting, co-host from 2004 or 2005); the text says only 'later with'.

The 'anecdote and reflection' description of public radio storytelling, fairness and right-of-reply expectations, and the glossary definitions (track, actuality, paper edit, room tone) are common usage and general practice, not checked against a glossary.
